1.name: Generosity
1.description: Any work you do here is for others. Act for others in small and large ways, its not about big occasional gestures but simply listening with Discernment.

2.name: Virtue
2.description: Virtue appears across traditions: Aristotle, Buddhism, and Christianity each list their own, mapping different routes to living well. At its core, virtue is excellence of character developed through practice—becoming the kind of person who reliably acts well because they've shaped themselves that way.

3.name: Stillness
3.description: Most of the time, for most of us, we feel like an out of control ChatGPT babbling in my head about every topic. If that's not happening it may then be some earworm song playing over and over. Stillness, when found may be the simplicty and relief you have been seeking. If may also be a life work to string together the small moments of stillness so it is with me more and more.

4.name: Discernment
4.description: We are looking for more presence, more attention and more fine-grained clarity. Check John Vervaeke's work on relevence realisation.

5.name: Conviction
5.description: The cemented decision to orient towards the values, deeds and actions that are my highest calling. Check Buddhhism's 'Right View'  and possibly 'Right Intention'.

6.name: Meditation
6.description: There are hundreds of style of meditation, some may advocate 'sitting and forgetting', some may urge 'self remembering', some may aim to increase discerment and others to instill generosity or good-will. Seek the practice that is healing and nourishing for the well-being of yourself and others around you. Its also possible that we don't DO meditation, it may be the stopping after all the other striving. A simple chance to (as they say) BE.

7.name: Goodfaith (Socratic) Dialog skills
7.description: Our media and social networks are filled with agression and drama, our schooling didn't teach us debate to discover a creative outcome, if we were taught debating, it was to win. Refer our posts on [Opponent Processing](https://djinoz.substack.com/p/tensegrity-and-opponent-processing?r=jy6d) and Beauty and the Beast.

8.name: Ritual
8.description: Perhaps we have always previously suspicious of Ritual as a mind-trick, especially conducted by some other party or organisation. That can be true, but Ritual can also help us get into the 'mood' for whatever we are undertaking. It might be an alter for meditation or prayer or it might be making a cup of coffee and a clean workspace before sitting down to do some drawing or writing. In other areas, it is also called 'Set and Setting' - that the environment is a container for you to do your best work.

9.name: Curiosity
9.description: Magic lies here within and children are masters. When we stop seeing something as a problem and get curious about how things are happening or what (if any) is an explanation of the situation and what may be a solution, we are starting the creative process. Refer David Deutsche about humans being [Universal Explainers and creators](https://djinoz.substack.com/p/third-force-blindness-part-1).

10.name: Awe/Wonder/Sacred
10.description: We may have confused an experience of the Sacred with only those things declared Sacred by organised religion. And so, our world has become more profane and we may feel there is nothing sacred in myself except for my children. But the sacred lies adjacent to creativity and discernment and, and, and...an initial First Bite of food is an invitation to the sacred. Interactions with nature are our most common experience of Awe and Wonder, now we can find them in other places when we actively give up our clinging to the profane.

11.name: Tech as a tool (not as a God)
11.description: When using tech, ask yourself 'what does this serve?' if its doom-scrolling it may not be in your best interests. I saw a recent video that frames technology impacts on a grid wisdom and agency: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n_iGN5kijvA

12.name: Gratitude Practice
12.description: Gratitude is an orientation, a conscious commitment to see the 'glass half full'. It also is cultivatable via in metta meditation, but here we have the opportunity to inject gratitude throughout the day. Some of us may have a 'joyful' default 'set-point', others may find that grumpiness or anxiety is our default state. Start by observing what is my most recurring mindset and wonder if there is something to be thankful for.

13.name: Delusion and Unskillful Actions
13.description: All your old habits belong to the past you, that retains the status quo. But you are cultivating a future you that may require letting go of what no longer serves. Buddhism identifies three poisons: greed, aversion, and delusion—the roots of unskillful action. Notice when your actions arise from these, rather than from wisdom and compassion. The practice isn't about perfection but about gradually recognizing and transforming patterns that create suffering for yourself and others.

14.name: Purpose
14.description: In the post-scarcity future, when basic needs are met by abundance, Purpose becomes the central question. Not 'what you do' for work, but 'how you appear' in the world—embodying the Fruits layer qualities of Conviction, Virtue, Generosity, Discernment, and Stillness. Your Purpose isn't found in a job title but in becoming the kind of person who reliably acts from wisdom and compassion, regardless of external circumstances. It's the answer to 'what do you stand for?' lived through daily practice.

15.name: Discomfort Resistance
15.description: The old saying *'no pain, no gain'* is probably correct in spirit but perhaps 'pain' is the **wrong view**. Any musician or sportsperson knows the discomfort that comes with discipline, the discipline that comes with mastering the craft. The linked video with Dr Anna Lembke expplains how a  healthy balance between pleasure and pain, fostering resilience and contentment.

16.name: Joy
16.description: 'If it's not big it doesn't count'. Do you think like that? Do you dismiss the hundreds of small accomplishments that you manage to complete every single day? Perhaps the simplest and most classic of these daily small accomplishments is to make your bed.

17.name: Be a Master of the Breath
17.description: Honestly, you could ignore most of the other faces of the dome and just watch your breath as your main wisdom practice. Initially we might discover its shallow and in the chest when we are feeling stressed. But through practice, we learn to breathe deeply from the belly, to notice the pause between breaths, to use breath as an anchor when the mind wanders. The breath is always available, a portable meditation object that travels with you everywhere. Master this one thing and much else follows.

18.name: Shadow
18.description: Not the one cast by the sun, but the emotional negativities, arguments, disgruntlements that may speak to you in your head and may distance you from your partner, family, friends, colleagues. Something that is powered by pain or disconnection or sense of self-worth.

19.name: Worship something greater than yourself
19.description: This phrase is a perennial reminder somewhat related to gratitude and may be found in awe. It might just be a great antidote to self-obsession and putting you in touch with a bigger picture, or the possibility of a greater cause. It could be something transcendent or it could be supporting a cause that you resonate with. Whatever it is, it breaks an inward spiral of drinking your own cool-aid.

20.name: First Principles Thinking
20.description: I'm not sure this is important, but we need a set of skills to be able to know we are self-deluded, or people are telling/selling us a story that is a deception. By thinking from first principles and overcoming our banana-brain biases and potentially exposing fallacies. Some readers may be offended in the linked article that uses a Musk example, but its useful to learn from. The big reference for cognitive biases is [Rationality: From AI to Zombies](https://elizier.neocities.org/), you can also get it in book form.

21.name: Low time preference (Long View)
21.description: The famous Stanford marshmallow experiment was a study on delayed gratification, an essential quality for working towards wisdom. 'The years teach much which the days never know.' — Ralph Waldo Emerson

22.name: Good Friends
22.description: Good mates yes, someone to listen. But also: Buddha, Dharma, Sangha. The latter is the community of like-minded friends who practice with us. In Christianity weekly Church provides a community contact for deep relationships or even social contact. Humans are social and connection with others is important for mental health but also reinforcement of the ethics, priorities and conviction - very few can do it alone.

23.name: Good Relationship
23.description: Your home life and/or a relationship of deep initimate trust.

24.name: Resolved Trauma
24.description: Trauma may carry such a strong emotional weight that it profoundly affects one's life - if unmanaged/unresolved, trauma could hamper progress in other areas.

25.name: Sleep
25.description: Every week it seems scientists report another study how critical 'good' sleep is to your cognition, wellbeing and even potential for dementia. Sleep hygiene advice is readily available and the current consensus is that 7 hours is good for most people. Old sayings like 'sleep is for the weak' or 'I will sleep when I am dead' are now empty hubris when our biology is running the show.

26.name: Upbringing
26.description: The environment and events of childhood may be supportive or challenging or tragic, we have to acknowledge its impact on our whole lives.

27.name: Sovereign Money
27.description: Money you control. In 2025 most people now know that governments create money when they can't balance the books. The standard 2-3% inflation is not a natural law, it is government and their reserve banks doing a Jedi Mind Trick on the population. So cash is weak money worth less every year...with compounding! In 2025 gold has shown itself as a better replacement than US dollars, gold's value has increased dramatically due to the perception that the US debt repayments can't be serviced without more money printing, or some kind of miracle from AI and robots. Bitcoin (and to a less extent, silver) is also attractive to people seeking sovereign money. Storing money in stock market assets may work for a while but is subject to bubbles and manipulation.

28.name: Inflamation & Gum Health
28.description: This seems ludicrous as something to consider, but now evidence is appearing that gum infections can lead to cancer. Large studies have found that severe periodontal disease is associated with a 24% increased risk of overall cancer, with more than double the risk for lung cancer and an 80% increased risk for colorectal cancer. Research tracking nearly 150,000 people found those with gum disease were 43% more likely to develop esophageal cancer and 52% more likely to develop gastric cancer Harvard Health—likely because oral bacteria and chronic inflammation may directly affect distant organs.

29.name: Sugar in Moderation
29.description: Perhaps this belongs with addictions (Delusion and Bad Habits), but, like smoking, the evidence is clear of the risks. YMMV.

30.name: Nutrition & Hydration
30.description: A statement of the obvious, perhaps.

31.name: Shelter
31.description: A safe and supportive living environment (as per Maslow). Strongly tied to Stable Society/Benevolent Gov but also related to mental health, poverty and domestic violence.

32.name: Connection to Nature
32.description: Increasingly city dwelling means that citizens lose contact with the natural world. The tech giants may hope that we fill our lives with screens, but 'touching grass', 'forest bathing', surfing, getting sunshine, immersion in water are all places that our biology evolved to flourish in. Don't neglect!

33.name: Stable Society/Benevolent Gov.
33.description: Just as we need shelter and nutrition, the country and society we live should support us. Hobbes' Leviathan defined a social contract to protect its citizens, this could be material but also mental health and affordability. See also Sovereign Money. The linked documentary provides a daunting explanation of what is common practice in manipulating the public.

34.name: What do you stand for?
34.description: I may not have an answer, the question may shock me. To start to find _some_ answer is to discover I've been drifting—that the question cuts deeper than any list of beliefs, demanding whether you've actually found or created something in myself worth defending. We should be centered to at least sense of what I value in myself and the world.

35.name: Courage and Survival Skills
35.description: Possibly 2 separate faces on the dome. Having appropriate skills for basic survival will give you confidence and hopefully seed courage. We are not talking about some false hubristic bravery but a humble preparation of you in nature. Courage is a much bigger topic - do I have the courage to speak my truth, to stand up for something? The more we get our sensory food from outside ourselves, the less centred we are and building a house of cards.

36.name: Tempered Addictions and Habits
36.description: We all have them, right?: Alcohol, stimulants, self-medication, need for drama, lust, doom scrolling etc. What do they serve in my life? Create boundaries around potentially addictive behaviors, such as limiting social media use or setting specific times for leisure activities. Don't read work emails when it is family/partner time or downtime. Don't use screens before bed.

37.name: Right Livelihood
37.description: From Buddhism's ethical conduct (Sila). Ask: is my way of making income supportive of my larger goals and for planet and its occupants? Do I conduct myself with respect and safety for others and my environment? If how you conduct yourself in the world lacks virtue it will become a burden for the other practices you may be seeking here, for example, sitting in meditation may be plagued by returning thoughts related to workplace conflicts or the goodness of what you do. In the old days, this might have related to being a butcher or a gangster (it's one of those 'thou shalt not kill' situations in Buddhism) but in the modern world we may expand this to other by products of hyper-scaled capitalism.

38.name: Physical Functioning
38.description: So far, science and AI havn't solved infinite longevity, therefore, the vehicle of our body has a finite time to support your goals and wishes. Everybody is dealt a unique set of cards, including physical disability, what can you do with it or transcending it?

39.name: Know the Mammal (Desires)
39.description: Humans are a big bundle of chemistry, conditioning and associations. This is why the Buddha identified 'craving' and 'aversion' as the 2nd Noble Truth - The Cause of Suffering.

40.name: 40 - Placeholder (an example)
40.description: You could add your own practices or qualities here.
